rv.q: This is not your typical overblown West End musical – and is all the better for it.
Not a resounding triumph, perhaps, but many aspects are bound to resonate.
What stands out from this frankly daft daisy chain of dalliances is the passionate score: sinuous, very beautiful and evoking love, wine and roses.
The truth is, though, that the years have been kinder to Ball than they have been to Aspects.
On the other hand, ‘Aspects of Love’ is such a seething ethical mess that it’s literally had to be rewritten to make its lead character seem less like a predatory paedophile.
But you sit through the two and a half hours hoping that the characters will acquire some sort of depth. They never do.
We get the sense that these people could only ever exist within the bounds of a musical – one that is easy enough to watch but entirely unconvincing in its emotions.
I found it all irredeemably icky, even if – much like herpes – its tunes won’t fail to linger.
And the whole thing feels off, like a day-old fish.
But it would take more than his golden-syrup vocals and twinkly charm to make wading through this sugary sludge worthwhile.

This production represents a gamble, too, and whatever one's reaction to the intractable nuttiness of the material, something about it - rather like a bygone, life-defining love affair - proves impossible to dismiss.
This is an astonishing feat of compressed storytelling.
It is a production that revels in its theatricality, even giving a couple of glimpses of the excellent band through the gauze at the rear of the stage.
If love really does change everything, perhaps it should have started with the plot, which will baffle some new audience members.
If you’re up for an expensive-looking, rather shallow, traditional musical with a great score and are ready to overlook a highly inappropriate plot, this is it.
You can certainly admire the efforts made here, while also questioning the wisdom of trying to stage such an inexorably dated – albeit occasionally beguiling – piece.
The narrative manages to feel both conventional and deeply, deeply weird.

cn.t: Lloyd Webber's chamber musical returns in a reworked revival that divides critics: some praise Ball's performance and the lush score, but many find the story creepy, dated, and problematic despite updates to its uncomfortable age-gap romances.

sg.ra: Closest and most direct view of the stage at Lyric Theatre, with the fullest sound. The standard top pick for any show here.
An elevated, full-stage view with no orchestra-level neck-craning — especially strong for shows with big staging or choreography.
A modest side angle on the stage but still close and clear — a reliable choice when center seats are sold out.

sg.vl: Good sound, check the seat map
sg.ra: Lyric Theatre's own seating notes flag possible obstructed views from the rear orchestra — sound still carries well, but check the seat map before booking here.
At 1,930 seats, Lyric Theatre is one of the larger Broadway houses — far side mezzanine seats sit well off-axis and a long way from the stage.

vs.sum: One of Broadway's largest houses (1,930 seats across four levels), the Lyric's sheer scale means rear orchestra and mezzanine seats sit far from the stage, with sightline obstructions from balcony overhangs. Acoustics are solid and the theater's modern construction makes it well-suited for spectacle productions.

acc.note: 42nd St entrance at street level with elevator to Orchestra and Dress Circle. No elevator to Balcony.
